newsitem.title: ITALY: MOTOR RACING-DRIVER MARTINI TESTIFIES AT SENNA TRIAL.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-DRIVER MARTINI TESTIFIES AT SENNA TRIAL.

text.p: Former Formula One driver Pierluigi Martini told a court on Wednesday that he and other drivers had reservations about the surface of the Imola racetrack before Ayrton Senna died in a crash there in 1994.
But the Italian, testifying as a prosecution witness at the manslaughter trial of six defendants including team boss Frank Williams, did not blame the circuit.
"For me the track didn't have anything to do with the accident," he told reporters later.

He did however say that the Tamburello bend where the Brazilian triple world champion died at the May 1 San Marino Grand Prix was a demanding stretch of track and acknowledged that there must have been a problem of some sort.
"A driver like Ayrton Senna wouldn't have left the track at that point unless there was some kind of problem," he said.
"A lot of things can happen in a race. In this particular case I don't know what happened," the Italian, called as an expert witness, told the court.

Those on trial are Frank Williams, Williams' team technical director Patrick Head, designer Adrian Newey, Belgian international race director Roland Bruynseraede and Imola officials Federico Bendinelli and Giorgio Poggi.
All six deny the charges of manslaughter.
Senna died when his Williams car left the track and hurtled into a concrete wall at around 210 kph.
Prosecutors blame a combination of mechanical failure and poor circuit design at the Tamburello.
Martini said he, Senna and others had noticed in the weeks before the race "a small bump" in the Tamburello bend which reduced a car's abilities to keep the racing line.
"There was a small bump in the middle that unsettled the cars. I, Senna and others mentioned it 15 days before the Grand Prix," he told the court.
"The racetrack officials were very efficient, they had it ground down a bit which was the only possible action but the situation only improved slightly," he added.
But Martini said that although the cars still grazed the surface with their aerodynamic side skirts, the drivers just needed to hold the correct line.
He said there was only one line into the Tamburello and the bump could not be avoided without going off the track.

Asked later whether such a bump could cause a steering column to break, Martini told reporters that he had never known one to. He also said that Senna's fast lap time seemed to indicate that his tyres were warmed up fully.
The Italian told the court that Senna had complained to him three weeks before the race that the handling of his car was "nervous" and there was little room for the driver.
